gallery.title: File:Ye Olde Curiosity Shop brochure circa 1907.jpg
gallery.artist: Ye Olde Curiosity Shop. Originally printed by the Kelly Printing Company.
gallery.description:
Ye Olde Curiosity Shop, Seattle, Washington. Circa 1907 brochure. Two photos of the interior of the shop and one of the exterior. 
Texts at bottom say "SEND A SOUVENIR TO YOUR FRIENDS", "Headquarters for Alaskan's and Globetrotters on the | Water Front, COLMAN DOCK | SEATTLE, WASHINGTON, USA | J. E. STANDLEY, Sole Proprietor", "EVERYBODY WELCOME".

gallery.filename: Ye Olde Curiosity Shop photo ad circa 1917.jpg
gallery.title: File:Ye Olde Curiosity Shop photo ad circa 1917.jpg
gallery.description:
Circa 1917 ad for Ye Olde Curiosity Shop, Seattle, Washington. The photo would be taken shortly after the shop moved back to Colman Dock, when the dock was remodeled 1916–1917. 
Founder J. E. Standley is visible in the doorway. Handwritten text across the bottom of the photo says "The most unique Shop in the World. On the Colman Dock Front, Seattle, U.S.A., foot of Columbia St. VISITORS ALWAYS WELCOME."

As the card indicates, the entryway was framed by the "Jaw bones of a whale. over 21 ft. in length."

gallery.title: File:Ye Olde Curiosity Shop 1901 montage.jpg
gallery.artist: Montage by J. E. Standley, based on images in books by Boas and Hoffman, as discussed above. The card in the middle is an ad for Standley's shop at the time.
gallery.description: Framed montage of photographs and drawings used by J. E. Standley in 1901 in his Seattle, Washington curio store that was the precursor to Ye Olde Curiosity Shop. Most of these images come either from Franz Boas's The Social Organization and the Secret Societies of the Kwakiutl Indians and Walter J. Hoffman's The Graphic art of the Eskimos.

gallery.filename: Hobbies Magazine J. E. Standley cover.jpg
gallery.title: File:Hobbies Magazine J. E. Standley cover.jpg
gallery.description: February–March 1919 Hobbies Magazine cover featuring a fireplace in the home of J. E. Standley, founder of Ye Olde Curiosity Shop (Seattle, Washington) flanked by objects similar to those he sold in the shop. The cover also shows two totem poles (one Haida and the other Tsimshian), presumably also from Standley's collection. Handwriting on the cover is Standley's.

gallery.filename: J. E. Standley Indian curio display 1905.jpg
gallery.title: File:J. E. Standley Indian curio display 1905.jpg
gallery.description: A display of Indian curios in the "Totem Place" home of J. E. Standley, founder of Ye Olde Curiosity Shop (Seattle, Washington). This image was used to illustrate an August 6, 1905 article in the Seattle Times. It was used to contrast the good care with which collectors such as Standley kept their collections of Indian artifacts to the poor job the University of Washington was doing at the time with its collection. Label and handwriting are Standley's: it looks like this may have been on a proper print of the photo, rather than a newspaper clipping.

gallery.filename: Perry Island postcard.jpg
gallery.title: File:Perry Island postcard.jpg
gallery.description:
Postcard of the U.S. revenue cutter Perry poses with Perry Island behind them. Perry Island was near Bogoslof Island in the Bering Sea. It arose in a volcanic eruption in 1906, witnessed by the crew of the Perry, and sank back under the sea about 5 years later.

The handwriting on the card is that of J. E. Standley, founder of Ye Olde Curiosity Shop (Seattle, Washington). The cards were for sale in the shop.

gallery.filename: Seattle - 4 totem poles Ravenna Park 1909.jpg
gallery.title: File:Seattle - 4 totem poles Ravenna Park 1909.jpg
gallery.description:
Cover of a brochure at the time of the Alaska-Yukon-Pacific Exposition (Seattle, Washington, 1909) advertising Seattle's Ravenna Park, then in private hands and also known as Big Tree Park. The totem poles shown were the work of Nuu-chah-nulth (Nootka) carvers, originally from Vancouver Island but living at the time in Seattle. The poles, commissioned by J. E. Standley, founder of Ye Olde Curiosity Shop, and sold to park owner W. W. Beck, became part of the Burke Museum collection in 1913.


In the picture, the poles have each been affixed into a niche in a tree.
